predictions.title: Selective-expert-checkpointing lands as default MoE save primitive by H2 2026
predictions.body: By the end of H2 2026 the consumer-tier MoE fine-tuning stack converges on selective-expert-checkpointing as the default save-time primitive across at least three of the major training frameworks, with Unsloth's v2026.5.26 release Tuesday establishing the operational template â€” checkpoint disk footprint for the MiniMax M2.7 235B MoE port collapsing from roughly 470GB to 188GB across the first ten saved revisions by freezing inactive expert columns on disk during write. The release is anchored by a paired Hugging Face Blog benchmark sheet from the Daniel Han Chen and Mike Han Chen author pair showing Qwen3.6-Max-Preview-235B training at roughly 1.74x throughput against the prior DeepSeek R3-Pro 38B recipe on a single 8x H200 SXM5 node, with peak combined VRAM falling 11.3 percent versus a vanilla Hugging Face Transformers v5 baseline. Two independent reproductions on CoreWeave and Crusoe Cloud 8x H200 SXM5 rentals landed inside 3 percent of the published numbers within the first trading day, and Simon Willison flagged the selective-expert-checkpoint primitive as the most operationally meaningful change shipped this quarter for downstream fine-tuners running against SSD budget caps on Lambda Labs or RunPod. The structural force is that once one mainstream trainer ships a save-time disk primitive that cuts MoE checkpoint footprint by ~60 percent without recipe rewrites and gets reproduced inside hours on multiple rental fleets, the rest of the consumer-tier training stack â€” Hugging Face TRL, Axolotl, Llama-Factory â€” has to either ship a compatible primitive or cede the 60B-to-235B-class MoE fine-tuning workload entirely, because the SSD-budget envelope is the binding constraint for paying tenants on Lambda Labs and RunPod once checkpoints cross the 200GB-per-revision line. Most likely landing is that by H2 2026 at least three of the major consumer-tier trainers (Unsloth plus two of TRL, Axolotl, or Llama-Factory) ship a save-time selective-expert-checkpoint primitive as a recipe-level default for MoE fine-tunes, with the contributed 60B-class-and-above recipe count crossing six across the cohort and at least one hyperscaler-managed fine-tuning service (AWS SageMaker, Google Vertex Custom Training, Azure ML) lighting up a managed tier that exposes it as a knob. Bear case is that one of the major trainers ships a competing block-sparse save format that fragments the standard before convergence, pushing the cross-trainer default into early 2027; absent that fragmentation, H2 2026 lands selective-expert-checkpointing as the de facto MoE save-time standard across the consumer-tier training cohort.

reasoning.because: Unsloth ships an expert-freeze checkpoint primitive cutting 235B MoE save disk ~60 percent.
reasoning.given: Two independent 8x H200 SXM5 reproductions landed inside 3 percent of the sheet within hours.
reasoning.so_that: Three or more consumer-tier trainers ship a save-time selective-expert primitive as MoE recipe default.
reasoning.landing: By H2 2026; Unsloth + two of TRL, Axolotl, Llama-Factory; one hyperscaler tier.
reasoning.plain_language: A new disk-saving trick for big MoE models shrinks save files about sixty percent, so other training tools will soon copy it.

predictions.summary: Unsloth's v2026.5.26 release ships a selective-expert-checkpoint primitive that cuts MiniMax M2.7 235B MoE checkpoint disk from ~470GB to ~188GB during save, with two independent 8x H200 SXM5 reproductions landing inside three percent. By H2 2026 three consumer-tier trainers default it.

predictions.title: SEC extends 8-K cyber materiality to agentic-AI dev-tool incidents by Q3 2026
predictions.body: By Q3 2026 the SEC publishes a staff statement or concept release that explicitly brings agentic-AI developer-tool incidents into the existing cybersecurity 8-K materiality regime first established under the December 2023 cyber-disclosure rule, with the Tuesday CISA-KEV listing of CVE-2026-46127 (the OpenAI Codex CLI prompt-injection-escalation flaw scored CVSS 9.4 with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation against a Fortune 500 financial-services customer per Mandiant) cited as the canonical reference incident the staff statement is drafted against. Three structural pressures push the SEC toward a near-term clarification. First, OpenAI is force-rolling every v3.1.x development tenant to the patched v3.1.10 inside a 72-hour window per its Tuesday security note, which means a large public-issuer population becomes presumptively patched-or-exposed by Friday and any issuer that has not disclosed by its next 10-Q cutoff is sitting on an exploitable-and-actively-exploited footprint in the agentic-tool layer of its development pipeline. Second, Mandiant's incident-response engagement at a named-vertical Fortune 500 financial-services customer is the exact fact-pattern shape the December 2023 rule was drafted against (a confirmed-exploitation incident at a public issuer in a sensitive vertical), and extending the four-business-day materiality clock into the AI-developer-tool tier is a clean precedential move rather than a novel one. Third, NIST NVD reclassified the vulnerability under a new agent-loader subcategory inside the same Tuesday afternoon update and Trail of Bits' agent-loader CVE taxonomy ticked up to twelve catalogued instances (the first net-new addition since the May 8 cycle), giving the SEC staff a stable structural taxonomy to anchor against rather than one it has to invent. The most likely landing is a Division of Corporation Finance staff statement issued inside Q3 2026 (after the comment cycle on the broader AI-disclosure rulemaking docket but before the Q4 earnings cycle), citing CVE-2026-46127 plus the Mandiant Fortune 500 engagement plus the agent-loader taxonomy as the structural justification, with at least one Big Four audit firm publishing a parallel client-advisory note inside the same week directing audit committees to add agentic-AI developer-tool exposure to their cyber-risk inventories. Bear case is the SEC folds the clarification into the broader AI-disclosure rulemaking and only the audit-advisory layer ships inside Q3 2026 with formal SEC guidance slipping to Q4; absent that deferral, Q3 2026 lands the agentic-AI developer-tool incident class explicitly inside the existing 8-K cyber disclosure regime.

reasoning.so_that: A Division of Corporation Finance staff statement extends the four-business-day clock to agentic-AI dev-tool incidents.
reasoning.landing: By Q3 2026; SEC staff statement plus Big Four audit-committee advisory.
reasoning.plain_language: A nasty bug in an AI coding tool let hackers into a major bank, so US regulators will soon make firms tell investors fast.

predictions.title: FFIEC adds agent-harness third-party risk addendum by Q3 2026
predictions.body: By Q3 2026 the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council publishes a focused addendum to the FFIEC Outsourcing Technology Services and Architecture, Infrastructure, and Operations booklets that explicitly extends bank third-party-risk supervision to agent-harness loaders and MCP-server channels, jointly signed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the FDIC, the NCUA, and the CFPB, with the addendum citing CVE-2026-46127 and the Mandiant Fortune 500 financial-services active-exploitation finding as the precipitating risk event. Tuesday's GitHub Security Lab advisory on CVE-2026-46127 in OpenAI's Codex CLI carried two operational features the prudential-supervisor cohort treats as activating triggers for a fresh booklet addendum rather than a footnote update inside an existing examination cycle: first, CISA's same-window placement of the CVE on the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog inside the Mandiant incident-response engagement at a Fortune 500 financial-services customer establishes a documented in-the-wild loss exposure at a supervised entity rather than a hypothetical risk surface, and second, NIST NVD's same-day reclassification under the new agent-loader subcategory lifts the Trail of Bits agent-harness CVE taxonomy to twelve cataloged instances which the booklet's existing third-party-risk taxonomy does not enumerate as a covered class. The structural force is that once a Fortune 500 supervised entity has a confirmed agent-harness in-the-wild exploitation event on the CISA KEV catalog with the underlying CVE class crossing into double-digit cataloged instances and NIST formally promoting a dedicated subcategory, the interagency cohort's standing examination workflow no longer has a defensible reading that agent-harness third-party-risk falls under the generic outsourced-technology-service framing â€” the booklet addendum becomes the cheapest compliance pathway for both the supervised entities and the supervisor staff conducting the next examination cycle. The most likely landing is the FFIEC publishing the addendum in a 60-90 day federal-register comment window opening inside the back half of June with a final version effective inside Q3 2026, the addendum naming the OWASP LLM Top 10 v2 prompt-injection and MCP-channel categories plus the Trail of Bits agent-harness CVE taxonomy as the canonical reference taxonomies for the agent-loader risk class, the FS-ISAC publishing a sector-coordinated playbook citing the addendum inside the same window, and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York including agent-harness third-party-risk in the next round of supervisory letters to the largest bank holding companies. Bear case is the interagency cohort defers a standalone booklet addendum and instead folds agent-harness third-party-risk into the next annual update to the existing Outsourcing booklet inside Q4 2026 with the addendum draft circulating as an informal interagency examination expectation through Q3; absent that fold-in, Q3 2026 lands the FFIEC addendum as the first prudential-regulator artifact that names agent-harness loaders as a supervised third-party-risk class.

reasoning.because: CVE-2026-46127 hits CISA KEV with Mandiant exploitation at a Fortune 500 bank customer.
reasoning.given: NIST NVD opens agent-loader subcategory; Trail of Bits taxonomy crosses twelve cataloged CVEs.
reasoning.so_that: FFIEC publishes booklet addendum naming agent-harness loaders and MCP channels as supervised risk class.
reasoning.landing: By Q3 2026; OCC, FRB, FDIC, NCUA, CFPB jointly sign; FS-ISAC playbook follows.
reasoning.plain_language: Bank regulators will write a new rule so banks must check the AI tools their vendors use, because hackers just broke in.

predictions.summary: CVE-2026-46127 in OpenAI Codex CLI hits CISA KEV with Mandiant confirming exploitation at a Fortune 500 bank customer, and NIST NVD opens a dedicated agent-loader subcategory. By Q3 2026 the FFIEC publishes a jointly signed addendum bringing agent-harness loaders under bank vendor-risk rules.
